5.0.0.en: The disciples of Ben Sirach believed in God, but he feared for them lest the enemy of good corrupt their faith. Therefore he took care to speak of arrogance as a sickness that creeps into the heart and mind of man, and deprives him of the spirit of humility toward people as toward God.

5.0.1.en: When Ben Sirach speaks to his young disciples, whom he is preparing to be scribes with their own role in the life of society, he knows that pride easily creeps in among some young people because of their sense of vitality and strength, and because of their progress in learning and culture beyond the previous generations and beyond their brothers of the present generation, so that they exaggerate their feeling of self-confidence. Instead of their self-confidence urging them to work seriously and positively for the advancement of society, they inwardly mock others, especially those who belong to the older generation.

5.0.2.en: Ben Sirach presented a set of prohibitions by repeating his words: "Do not...", warning us of the spiritual dangers that arrogance causes [1-9].

5.0.3.en: On the other hand, it is hard for a person to discover his own self-deception, for in theory he believes that the Lord is God, while in practice he sets up other gods for himself. The sources of self-deception are the following:

5.0.4.en: A. Money is his god [1]: He warns against exaggerated reliance on money. By his purely human calculations he feels able to manage all his affairs with money, and has no need to believe in God, nor of any human being.

5.1.0.en: B. His gods are the satisfaction of pleasures and passions as a source of happiness and satiety [2]. False security rests on haughtiness and conceit, relying on wealth, while human lusts lead a person into error.

5.1.1.en: C. Misunderstanding God's long-suffering [3-6], on the ground that God has never yet punished him for his sins, together with ignorance of the meaning of joyful hope and a false reliance on the greatness of His mercy [6]. It is not fitting to exalt oneself against God, for man cannot stand before God [3].

5.2.0.en: D. Putting off until tomorrow [7]. The wise man warns us against postponing repentance, lest God's wrath come suddenly upon man.

5.2.1.en: Do not let your heart rely on your wealth, and do not say: "It is enough for me" [1].

5.2.2.en: He warns us against being preoccupied with wealth and relying on it while ignoring trust in God, a matter that is dangerous to the soul. St. John Chrysostom says: [Money is of no benefit if the soul is poor, and poverty does no harm if the soul is rich.[1]]

5.2.3.en: Do not follow your own desire and your strength, to walk according to the lusts of your heart [2].

5.2.4.en: It is good for a person to take pride in the abilities for thinking and managing that have been given to him, and in the possibility of carrying out the divine commandment; but pride corrupts these gifts, for he behaves haughtily, supposing that all things go in a way that satisfies his lusts and passions. Sadly, he who follows his own desire may carry out the commandment outwardly, but without sincerity of heart?

5.2.5.en: v He who carries out God's commandment without sincerity is not forbidden. In appearance he remains like one who fulfils the Lord's teaching with all uprightness. And although no one sins because of this work itself, and some may even benefit from it, such a person must be advised, so that his motives may agree with his good work... (The Apostle Paul gives us a practical example) "Some indeed preach Christ even of envy and strife; and some also of good will: The one preach Christ of contention, not sincerely, supposing to add affliction to my bonds: But the other of love, knowing that I am set for the defence of the gospel. What then? notwithstanding, every way, whether in pretence, or in truth, Christ is preached; and I therein do rejoice, yea, and will rejoice" (Phil 1:15-18)[2].

5.2.6.en: St. Basil the Great: And do not say: "Who is the master who rules over me?", for the Lord will surely punish you [3].

5.2.7.en: A person may look at the success he has reached in his life, and in haughtiness feel that God has no authority over him, ignoring the great day of the Lord. The prophet says: "For, behold, the day cometh, that shall burn as an oven; and all the proud, yea, and all that do wickedly, shall be stubble: and the day that cometh shall burn them up, saith the Lord of hosts, that it shall leave them neither root nor branch" (Mal 4:1).

5.2.8.en: v Flee from pride, for it is the most deceptive of the sicknesses of the soul. From it spring evil desire, the love of money, hatred, wars and conflicts. For those who covet obtaining more than they have will not be able to stop. Their desire springs only from their love of displaying their achievements...

5.2.9.en: If we are able to cut off pride, the head of every evil, it will be accompanied by the possibility of putting to death all the other members of evil. Then nothing will prevent us from living on earth as though it were heaven!...

5.2.10.en: If we wish to acquire glory, we must flee from the glory of the world and desire glory from God alone. Then we shall attain both together (glory in the world and from God), and enjoy them by the grace and tender love of our Lord Jesus Christ[3].

5.3.s.en: Do not despise the long-suffering of God

5.3.0.en: Do not say: "I have sinned, and what has happened to me?", for the Lord is slow to anger [4].

5.3.1.en: Some misunderstand God's long-suffering toward them, and think that talk of the Lord's discipline of sinners is imaginary and unrealistic ideas. This assurance is false and deceives the soul, and drives a person to postpone repentance. St. Paul the Apostle says: "Or despisest thou the riches of his goodness and forbearance and longsuffering; not knowing that the goodness of God leadeth thee to repentance?" (Rom 2:4).

5.3.2.en: v The prophet says: "I sin, what has happened to me?" as though he were saying: Surely God will not know my sins, since He does not punish me and discipline me at once. Again the person thinks: "God forgets me, He hides His face, and now He sees (my sins)" (cf. Ps 10:11) LXX. When he says: "God forgets me", he judges that the long-suffering of Him who forgives sins is in truth neglect (on God's part). He counts God's long-suffering as an omission on God's part, whereas in truth the gentleness of God's ordering of justice has left the matter to a later time[4].

5.4.0.en: Faustus of Riez: v If the judgment on sins committed in ignorance is so severe, and they need a sacrifice to atone for them, a truth to which Job bore witness by offering a sacrifice for his children, what shall be said of those who commit sin knowingly, or those who in their silence consent to the sinful conduct of others?[5]

5.4.1.en: St. Basil the Great: Do not be confident of obtaining forgiveness, so as to add sin upon sin [5].

5.5.0.en: v Since we do not know when or at what time we shall be taken from this world, let us hasten, without delay or postponement, to move from the left side to the right. It is fitting that we not trust in health or in the years of our life. For the person who is never sure of his life hastens to seek the medicine of his salvation[6].

5.6.0.en: Father Caesarius, Bishop of Arles: v He says "he will despise the other" (Mt 6:24) without saying "hate him", because a person often cannot hate God, but holds Him in contempt, that is, does not fear Him, as though feeling the abundance of God's mercies. But the Holy Spirit removes that destructive outlook, for He says through the prophet: "My son, add not sin to sin, and say not, His mercy is great" (cf. Sir 5:5-6). "Not knowing that the goodness of God leadeth thee to repentance" (Rom 2:4). For who is as merciful as God, who forgives all the sins of those who return to Him, and makes the wild olive tree a partaker of the fatness of the olive tree, and likewise who is as severe as He, so as to break off the natural branches for their unbelief? (Rom 11:17-24)[7].

5.6.1.en: St. Augustine: And do not say: "His mercy is great, He will forgive the multitude of my sins", for both mercy and wrath come from Him, and His indignation rests upon sinners [6].

5.7.0.en: v Many very negligent persons use God's compassion as a pretext to increase the guilt of their sins, and carry their negligence to excess, saying: "There is no Gehenna, there is no punishment to come. God forgives us all our sins." To shut their mouths the wise man says: "Say not, His mercy is great; He will be pacified for the multitude of my sins" (Sir 5:6), and also: "As his mercy is great, so is his correction also" (cf. Sir 16:12)[8].

5.8.0.en: v If the laws of men must be observed carefully, how much more the laws of God. Someone says: "But He is good." How long shall we utter this foolish speech? I say it is foolish, not because God is not good, but because of holding on to the thought that His goodness is in our hands for this purpose... Listen to the Holy Scripture, which says: "Say not, His mercy is great; He will be pacified for the multitude of my sins" (Sir 5:6). It does not forbid us to say that His mercy is great. This is not what it commands us; rather it calls us to say this continually... It says this only so that we may not despair because of our sins, but repent. For the goodness of God leads us to repentance (Rom 2:4), not to a greater evil[9].

5.8.1.en: v Are you an old man, and the time of your departure from the world has come? Do not think that even in this you are deprived of repentance. Do not despair of your salvation! Consider how the thief was set free while on the cross; what time is shorter than that hour in which he was crowned?! Yet this was enough for his salvation.

5.8.2.en: Are you a young person? Do not trust in your youth, and do not think that you are guaranteed some time to live in this life. For "the day of the Lord so cometh as a thief in the night" (1 Thess 5:2). He has made our end unseen (unknown), so that we may exert effort and look ahead clearly.

5.8.3.en: Do you not see people being taken day after day before their time?! For this reason the wise man advised us, saying: "Make no tarrying to turn to the Lord, and put not off from day to day" (cf. Sir 5:7). Lest you delay at any time and perish.

5.9.0.en: Let the old man keep this counsel, and let the young man receive this advice. Yes. You are now in safety. Are you rich, with abundant wealth, and no sorrows touch you? Hear what St. Paul the Apostle says: "For when they shall say, Peace and safety; then sudden destruction cometh upon them" (1 Thess 5:3)[10].

5.10.0.en: v "For God sent not his Son into the world to condemn the world; but that the world through him might be saved" (Jn 3:17). Many of these people tend to add sin upon sin and misuse God's mercy, and so plunge into grievous negligence, saying such words as: "There is no Gehenna, and there is no judgment; God forgives all our sins." So to silence them the wise man says: "Say not, His mercy is great; He will be pacified for the multitude of my sins: for mercy and wrath come from him, and his indignation resteth upon sinners" (cf. Sir 5:6); and also: "As his mercy is great, so is his correction also" (cf. Sir 16:12)[11].

5.10.1.en: St. John Chrysostom: v He who said: "If the wicked will turn from all his sins that he hath committed... all his transgressions that he hath committed, they shall not be mentioned unto him" (Ezek 18:21-22), also said: "Make no tarrying to turn to the Lord" (Sir 5:7).

5.10.2.en: If the first promise makes you secure, the second request gives you a reason to strive. Listen to the divine Scriptures, for they say: "Remember that death will not be slow" (Sir 14:12).

5.11.0.en: "Say not, His mercy is great; He will be pacified for the multitude of my sins: for mercy and wrath come from him, and his indignation resteth upon sinners" (Sir 5:6), that is, those who persist in their sins. If we observe this with sincerity and care, and have recourse to repentance without postponement, we shall be able to escape eternal punishment and gladly obtain eternal rewards[12].

5.12.s.en: The danger of presumption and despair [7]

5.12.0.en: In the spirit of wisdom, it is fitting for the believer neither to misuse hope in God's mercies by being slack in returning to God by repentance, nor to have his soul shattered by despair because of the multitude or the hideousness of his sins. For false hope, like despair, is a dangerous sickness that must be treated.

5.12.1.en: v What then does the Lord do with those who are exposed to danger from these two sicknesses?

5.12.2.en: To those who are endangered by hope He says this: "Make no tarrying to turn to the Lord, and put not off from day to day: for suddenly shall the wrath of the Lord break forth, and in thy security thou shalt be destroyed, and perish in the day of vengeance" [7]. And to those who are endangered by despair, what does He say? "His transgressions I will not remember" (Ezek 18:21-22).

5.13.0.en: Therefore, because of those exposed to the danger of despair, He offers them the harbor of forgiveness; and because of those exposed to the danger of hope and deceived by postponement, He made the day of death uncertain. You do not know when the last day will come. Are you ungrateful, when you have today in your hand to set your affairs right?[13]

5.13.1.en: St. Augustine: Make no tarrying to turn to the Lord, and put not off from day to day.

5.13.2.en: For suddenly shall the wrath of the Lord break forth, and you shall perish in the day of vengeance [7].

5.14.0.en: St. Augustine reveals the war of the enemy of good, the devil, with some people in his time. The enemy begins by resisting the Christian faith and casting doubt on it. But when some discovered the loftiness and holiness of the Christian faith and the enemy could not make them doubt, he began to present to them the loftiness and holiness of the faith in a terrifying way, so that they would delay returning to the Lord, accepting the faith and confessing their sins, and so they went on postponing from day to day without taking a serious step toward meeting the Savior[14].

5.14.1.en: v The mind wavers between presumption and despair. You must fear lest presumption kill you; and fear also lest you do this without regard for God's mercy, and fall under judgment. Likewise you must fear lest despair kill you when you think of the terrible sins you have committed, that they have no forgiveness. In this way you do not come to repentance, but instead fall under the sentence of Wisdom: "I also will laugh at your calamity" (Prov 1:26).

5.14.2.en: How does the Lord treat those who are in danger from these two sicknesses? For those in danger from presumption, He says: "Make no tarrying to turn to the Lord, and put not off from day to day: for suddenly shall the wrath of the Lord break forth, and in thy security thou shalt be destroyed, and perish in the day of vengeance" (cf. Sir 5:7). For those in danger from despair, He (the Lord) offers us the refuge of forgiveness.

5.15.0.en: For those who are in danger because of presumption and who lead themselves astray by postponement, the Lord made the day of death unknown. For you do not know when the last day will come upon you. You are an ungrateful man. Why do you not make use of today as a gift from God given for your repentance?[15]

5.16.0.en: v What shall I say of the many grave evils, the things known to the public, which they have inferred from your conduct since your marriage? You are a Christian, you have a conscience, and you fear God. Look into yourself, and you will find what I hesitate to utter because of the many evils for which you must offer repentance. I believe this is the reason why the Lord has left you until now, and rescued you from all dangers, that perhaps you may be sorry for what you have done, but on condition that you listen to what is written: "Make no tarrying to turn to the Lord, and put not off from day to day" (cf. Sir 5:7)[16].

5.17.0.en: v Hear the Holy Scripture: "I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked; but that the wicked turn from his way and live" (Ezek 33:11). By these words of God he turns back to hope, but there is a snare to be feared, lest through this hope a person sin all the more. What else do you say, you who through hope sin all the more? "When I return, God will forgive me everything, so let me do now what I please." Do not say: "Tomorrow I shall return, tomorrow I shall please God, and He will forgive me all the deeds of today and yesterday." You speak the truth: God promises forgiveness for your conduct, but He has not promised you that you will have tomorrow when you postpone (repentance)[17].

5.18.0.en: St. Augustine: v One advises us: "Put not off from day to day" (cf. Sir 5:7). By this you can succeed in most matters. And by this you manage well all the affairs of your house for yourself."[18].

5.18.1.en: v Let the young man take into account the uncertainty (of the time) of death. It often happens that many old men continue here while the young are carried off (to death) before them. For this reason no schedule has been set for our death, but it has been left uncertain. Therefore the wise man advises: "Make no tarrying to turn to the Lord, and put not off from day to day", "for thou knowest not what a day may bring forth" (cf. Sir 5:7; Prov 27:1). For postponement carries danger and fear, while not postponing reveals salvation in safety[19].

5.18.2.en: St. John Chrysostom: v Those who have no natural inclination toward the good must not lose heart nor despair, but must not cease striving toward the virtuous life that pleases God, however difficult it may seem to them to reach or attain it[20].

5.18.3.en: St. Anthony the Great: v In truth, no one should delay for a long time in his sins, relying on his hope in God's mercies, since no one desires to remain sick in body for a long time because of his hope of obtaining health in the future... The blessed David says: "Today if ye will hear his voice, harden not your hearts" (Ps 95:7-8). And the blessed Paul says: "Take heed, brethren, lest there be in any of you an evil heart of unbelief, in departing from the living God. But exhort one another daily, while it is called To day; lest any of you be hardened through the deceitfulness of sin" (Heb 3:12-13). Therefore he lives with a hardened heart who either does not return, despising the forgiveness of his sins, or who hopes for God's mercy when the end of the present life has come while he continues in his persistence in his crimes[21].

5.18.4.en: Fulgentius: v With thoroughly effective counsel, dearly beloved, and with kindness, the Lord advises us with fatherly tenderness when the prophet says: "Make no tarrying to turn to the Lord, and put not off from day to day" (cf. Sir 5:7). "Thou knowest not what a day may bring forth" (Prov 27:1). "Between morning and evening the time is changed" (cf. Sir 18:26). In another place we were also advised with an effective commandment: "Walk while ye have the light, lest darkness come upon you" (Jn 12:35).

5.18.5.en: A careless person may say: When I reach old age I shall have recourse to the medicine of repentance. The wretched man does not know that if he becomes accustomed to committing sins with the promise of repentance, he deceives himself, for it leads him into an evil life for a long time, so that only with suffering can he become fit to obtain the fruit of repentance[22].

5.19.0.en: 10 Do not rely on wealth gained by injustice, for it will profit you nothing in the day of vengeance. 11 Do not turn with every wind, and do not walk in every way; for so does the sinner who has a double tongue. 12 But be steadfast in your understanding, and let your speech be one. 13 Be swift to hear, and slow to give an answer. 14 If you have understanding, answer your neighbor; if not, lay your hand upon your mouth. 15 In speech is honor and dishonor, and the tongue of man is his ruin. 16 Be not called a whisperer, and do not lie in wait with your tongue. 17 For shame is upon the thief, and a severe reproach upon the double-tongued. 18 Be not ignorant in a great matter or in a small.

5.19.1.en: Ben Sirach offers us the following practical counsels:

5.19.2.en: A. Rejecting wealth gained by injustice [8]. B. Not wavering between ways [9].

5.19.3.en: C. Care for the holiness of thought and word [10-14]. D. Guarding against rapid inconstancy [15].

5.19.4.en: Do not rely on wealth gained by injustice, for it will profit you nothing in the day of distress [8].

5.19.5.en: Do not be winnowed with every wind, and do not walk in every way, for so does the sinner who has a double tongue [9].

5.19.6.en: The Lord Christ praised John the Baptist because he was steadfast and not wavering: "What went ye out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken with the wind?" (Mt 11:7). And in the epistle of our teacher James the Apostle it is written: "A double minded man is unstable in all his ways" (Jas 1:8).

5.19.7.en: Be steadfast in your understanding, and let your speech be consistent [10].

5.20.0.en: Be swift to hear, and patient in answering [11].

5.20.1.en: As to speech, it is fitting for the believer to be quick to listen and slow to answer. Speaking with wisdom is the way of honor, while the double-tongued becomes fit for shame and severe judgment.

5.20.2.en: v "My mouth shall speak of wisdom; and the meditation of my heart shall be of understanding."

5.20.3.en: Since, according to the Apostle: "With the heart man believeth unto righteousness; and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation" (Rom 10:10), the work of both in human beings indeed suggests perfection. Therefore the passage joined the two together in the same place, the work of the mouth and the meditation of the heart. Indeed, if goodness had not been stored up beforehand in the heart, how could one who has not acquired it in secret show the treasure through his mouth? And if he has good things in his heart, but we do not do these openly by speaking, it is said to him: "Wisdom that is hid, and treasure that is not seen, what profit is in them both?" Let my mouth speak of wisdom, and for my advancement let my heart meditate upon prudence.

5.20.4.en: "I will incline mine ear to a parable: I will open my dark saying upon the harp psaltery" (Ps 49:4).

5.20.5.en: The prophet still presents his own person, so that his words may not be despised as though offered by human invention. He says: What I teach is from the (Holy) Spirit, this I declare to you, and I utter nothing of my own, nothing human. But since I hear the dark sayings of the Spirit, who sends down the wisdom of God mysteriously, I disclose and reveal the dark sayings to you. Moreover, I reveal nothing else through the harp psaltery. The harp is a musical instrument that makes its sound heard in harmony with the melody of the voice.

5.20.6.en: Accordingly, the rational harp is laid open, especially at that time when the works play in harmony with the words. For he who does what he teaches is a spiritual harp. It is he who discloses the dark sayings in the Psalm, and prepares the possibility of teaching as a model. Therefore, since he knows that there is nothing discordant or out of tune in his life, he utters with confidence the following words: "Wherefore should I fear in the days of evil, when the iniquity of my heels shall compass me about?" (Ps 49:5). By the day of evil he means the day of judgment, of which it was said: "The day of the Lord is incurable, upon all the nations" (cf. Isa 13:9), of which the prophet says: "His plots trouble everyone."

5.20.7.en: At that time, then, since I have done nothing against the Law in the way of life, I do not fear the day of evil. For the marks of sinners do not stand around me nor trouble me; accusations rise against me in silent charges.

5.20.8.en: No one stands as an accuser against you but yourself, or your very works; each deed stands in its form, adultery and theft and fornication, as by night, with the particular circumstances that show its features, and in general every sin is present with its mark, bearing a clear remembrance.

5.20.9.en: The marks of sinners, then, do not trouble me, for I incline my ear to a parable, I disclose my dark sayings upon the harp[23].

5.21.0.en: St. Basil the Great: If you know something, answer your neighbor's question, and if not, lay your hand upon your mouth [12].

5.21.1.en: It is a sign of sincerity with oneself to cease answering vain questions, which distract the mind, occupy it with what is of no benefit, and waste time.

5.21.2.en: v "And when they had found him on the other side of the sea, they said unto him, Rabbi, when camest thou hither?" (Jn 6:25); this passage shows a scene of friends expressing a delicate matter. At any rate some elements seem meaningless, even childish. It was really fitting for them not to speak with the great Teacher about trivial matters, but to ask Him in order to learn something. What need was there to ask when He had come there? Or what benefit would they gain from knowing it? For this reason we must seek wisdom from the wise, and keep a watchful silence rather than enter into unsuitable conversations.

5.21.3.en: The Apostle urges us to have our speech seasoned with salt (Col 4:6). And another wise man calls us to something similar: "If thou hast understanding, answer thy neighbor; if not, lay thy hand upon thy mouth" (Sir 5:12). We learn also in another place how we are judged for any careless utterance: "If any man among you seem to be religious, and bridleth not his tongue, but deceiveth his own heart, this man's religion is vain" (Jas 1:26)[24].

5.22.0.en: St. Cyril the Great: In speech there is glory and dishonor, and the fall of man is caused by his tongue [13].

5.23.0.en: Beware of being called a slanderer, and do not lay an ambush with your tongue, for shame awaits the thief, and the judgment upon the double-tongued is grave [14].

5.23.1.en: Slander reflects the slanderer's preoccupation, away from his own sins, with exposing the sins of others, even if in secret. For judging means that we do not love others, while we usurp the right of God, the only Judge. Therefore Ben Sirach sees slander and judging as plunder and theft, which shame overtakes on the day of judgment.

5.23.2.en: "The double-tongued": By the two tongues he means hypocrisy, in which a person appears otherwise than he is within, or appears with two different personalities. The society of mankind is a field founded on true wisdom. For human life at all its levels rests on the mutual relations of human beings with one another in mutual trust; so if a person feels that his brother is deceitful and not upright in his thought, words and conduct, speaking with two tongues, he loses trust in him.

5.24.0.en: Do not sin in great matters or small [15].

5.24.1.en: v Question: How should one deal with those who avoid the great sins and are careless about the lesser sins?

5.24.2.en: Answer: First of all it must be understood that this distinction has no basis in the New Testament. One declaration was made concerning all sins, when the Lord says: "Whosoever committeth sin is the servant of sin" (Jn 8:34)... If we can safely speak of a small sin and a great sin, there is a testimony that is not accepted, namely to argue with anyone that the great sin is that which seizes a person under its dominion, while the small is that which does not gain the upper hand, as with wrestlers, for the stronger is the victor, and the weaker is defeated by the greater, whoever he may be[25].

5.24.3.en: St. Basil the Great: Inspired by Sirach 5

5.25.s.en: Our living faith and the life of uprightness

5.25.0.en: v What shall we render to You, O Lord, for the multitude of Your benefits?

5.25.1.en: Your grace gives us the faith that works by love.

5.25.2.en: Your grace shapes our depths, that we may truly become Your icon.

5.25.3.en: Your grace shatters all the deceptions of the enemy, so we shall not walk with him in the way of arrogance.

5.25.4.en: Shine with the light of Your knowledge in my depths, so that the love of money may not occupy my heart, and lusts and pleasures may not inflame my emotions.

5.25.5.en: You alone satisfy my soul, O desire of my heart!

5.25.6.en: I shall not covet money, even if the treasures of the world were offered to me.

5.25.7.en: And no lust will draw me away while You dwell in me.

5.25.8.en: v I find Your commandment sweet, for it pours some of Your splendor upon my soul.

5.25.9.en: It adorns me, and prepares me as a heavenly bride.

5.25.10.en: Your authority is the perfection of freedom.

5.25.11.en: So the evil one cannot creep into me and enslave my will, my heart, my mind and my senses.

5.25.12.en: Glory to You, O wonderful Liberator!

5.25.13.en: I rejoice whenever You set my brothers free from the bondage of the devil and his evil works.

5.25.14.en: O You who are wonderful in Your humility, shatter all pride that creeps into me.

5.25.15.en: Your dwelling in me turns my heart into a heaven.

5.25.16.en: He who cleaves to You experiences the pledge of heaven, and finds in the world no glory or money that entices him.

5.25.17.en: v You are wonderful in Your long-suffering toward me, O Holy One!

5.25.18.en: You know my hidden and open sins, and You cannot bear them.

5.25.19.en: By Your grace I shall not despise Your long-suffering toward me.

5.25.20.en: Let me hasten to You, and grant me sincere repentance, so that I may not be lax with sin.

5.25.21.en: Let me prepare for the meeting with You with joy and gladness, without postponement, even for a moment!

5.25.22.en: Your mercy is exceedingly great, urging me to cleave to You at once!

5.25.23.en: Grant me neither to despair because of the multitude of my sins, nor to be lax in hastening to repentance.

5.25.24.en: By Your love You have filled our hearts with hope, however great our sins, and by Your care You have asked us not to postpone, lest the enemy creep up on us and deceive us.

5.25.25.en: You have opened for us a harbor of salvation to remove our slackness from us!

5.25.26.en: v Sanctify, O Lord, all the steps of my life. For in You I walk the straight way without deviation.

5.25.27.en: You are the way, the truth and the life.

5.25.28.en: Grant me Your righteousness, so that I may wrong no one.

5.25.29.en: Hold my hand, that I may cleave to You always.

5.25.30.en: Sanctify my mind, and set a guard upon my mouth.

5.25.31.en: Grant me steadfastness in You, that I may not move away from You; grant me to be swift to hear and slow to answer.

5.25.32.en: v Sanctify my tongue, O Lord, that I may not be a slanderer, lest I be occupied with exposing the sins of my brothers instead of my own sins.

5.25.33.en: And let me not be a hypocrite with two tongues, so that what my tongue speaks is different from what my mind thinks and from what my heart utters in secret.
